statement: In one small echocardiography study of young adults in Belgium (Droogmans et al., 2007), heart valve findings that met the US Food and Drug Administration's criteria for valve disease caused by appetite-suppressant drugs (mitral regurgitation of grade 2 of 4 or more, or aortic regurgitation of grade 1 of 4 or more) were found in 8 of 29 people who had taken MDMA for at least 6 months (28 in 100; 95% interval 15 to 46, editors' calculation) and in 0 of 29 age- and sex-matched students who reported no drug use (Fisher's exact test, p = 0.0045). The people who had taken MDMA reported, by interview, a mean of 3.6 tablets a week (standard deviation 6.7) for a mean of 6.1 years (3.4), figures given for the 33 people recruited and not the 29 scanned. The leaks were usually mild to moderate. The clearest differences were in the tricuspid valve, with regurgitation of grade 2 of 4 or more in 13 of 29 against 0 (p < 0.001), and in stiffened (restrictive) mitral valve motion, 7 of 29 against 0 (p = 0.01). The two parts of the definition were not clear on their own: mitral regurgitation of grade 2 of 4 or more (4 of 29 against 0) and aortic regurgitation of grade 1 of 4 or more (4 of 29 against 0), p = 0.11 for each. Thin filaments called strands on the aortic valve were found in 5 of 29 against 0 (p = 0.05). People with higher grades had reportedly taken more tablets in total (943 against 242, p = 0.03; group sizes not given). The study cannot show that MDMA caused these findings: the valves were scanned once, so there is no scan from before MDMA use (one of the limits the authors state); the people who had taken MDMA came from psychiatry departments and drug-help centres and the controls from student advertisements, matched only on age and sex; other drug use is not reported although the authors note that substance use is mostly not limited to one drug; the amount came from interview and the paper reports no analysis of what the tablets held; 4 of the 33 people recruited were excluded after scanning; the study is small; and nobody had a history of heart disease or needed valve surgery, so it says nothing about symptoms or illness. The authors cite a cell-culture study (second-hand here) in which MDMA activated the 5-HT2B receptor and made human valve cells multiply, in a way the authors call fenfluramine-like; this study did not test that mechanism.
plain: In one small Belgian study, 8 of 29 young adults who had taken MDMA for at least six months (by their own account, on average about 4 tablets a week for about 6 years) had mitral or aortic valve findings that met a US definition of drug-related valve disease, against none of 29 students who reported using no drugs. Most of the leaks were mild or moderate. The biggest gap was in the valve on the right side of the heart (the tricuspid valve, which that definition does not cover), where 13 of 29 had a leak of grade 2 of 4 or more, against none. People with higher grades of leak said they had taken more tablets in total; the paper does not give the group sizes. This does not show that MDMA caused it: each person was scanned once and nobody before starting, the two groups were recruited differently (psychiatry departments and drug-help centres against student advertisements), other drug use is not reported, and the amount of MDMA came from what people said. The study did not check what the tablets held and says nothing about symptoms or illness.
population: Young adults in Brussels and Flanders (mean age about 24 to 26; 45% women): 29 who had taken MDMA for at least 6 months in the past year, recruited from psychiatry departments of two hospitals and from help centres for people with drug problems, and 29 age- and sex-matched students with no drug use; none with a history of heart disease or of ergot, appetite-suppressant or intravenous drug use
exposure: Self-reported MDMA use for at least 6 months, by interview (mean 3.6 tablets a week for 6.1 years among the 33 people recruited); tablets not analysed
comparator: 29 age- and sex-matched students who reported no drug use
outcome: Valve findings on echocardiography read blind by two observers: FDA criteria for drug-induced valve disease (mitral regurgitation of 2/4 or more, or aortic regurgitation of 1/4 or more), regurgitation by valve, restrictive motion and strands
magnitude: FDA-criteria valve disease: 8 of 29 (28%; Wilson 95% interval 15% to 46%, editors' calculation) against 0 of 29 (upper 95% bound about 12%, editors' calculation), Fisher p = 0.0045 (the editors' recalculation reproduces the printed p values). By valve, MDMA group against controls (counts of 29): tricuspid regurgitation 2/4 or more 13 (45%) against 0, p < 0.001, mean regurgitant area ratio 19% (SD 9.5) against 9% (SD 4.5), p < 0.001; mitral 2/4 or more 4 (14%) against 0, p = 0.11, mean area ratio 12% (SD 9.8) against 5% (SD 1.3), p < 0.007; aortic 1/4 or more 4 (14%) against 0, p = 0.11; pulmonary 1/4 or more 14 (48%) against 10 (34%), p = 0.42; restrictive motion mitral 7 (24%) against 0, p = 0.01, tricuspid 5 (17%) against 1 (3%), p = 0.19; strands aortic 5 (17%) against 0, p = 0.05, mitral 1 (3%) against 0. Cumulative tablets 943 (SD 1,162) in people with mitral or tricuspid regurgitation of 2/4 or more or any aortic regurgitation against 242 (SD 212) in the rest, p = 0.03. The printed relative risks (for example 1.68, 5.83) are not interpretable as risk ratios and are not used.

evidence.extracted: Recruitment: people who had taken MDMA in the past year were recruited from the psychiatry departments of two general hospitals and from help centres for people with drug problems in Brussels and Flanders, Belgium, between December 2004 and February 2006; all took part voluntarily with written consent. Because substance use is mostly not limited to one drug, an experienced psychiatrist interviewed each person about current and past drug use (the paper does not report what the interviews found). People with a history of ergot-derived drugs, Chinese herbs, appetite-suppressant drugs, intravenous drugs or any drug known to induce valve disease were excluded, as were people with any past cardiac disease, congenital or degenerative valve disease (including mitral or tricuspid prolapse) found on echocardiography, or poor image quality. Controls were age- and sex-matched students who answered advertisements and reported no drug use, with the same exclusions.

evidence.locator: Methods, 3rd to 5th paragraphs; Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 1443)
evidence.extracted: Examinations were done by experienced sonographers who were not told the person's identity; images were stored, randomized and read blind by one sonographer and one independent observer, whose agreement on the FDA criteria was excellent (kappa above 0.9) and whose data were used. Valve disease was defined by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) criteria for appetite-suppressant-induced valve disease: mitral regurgitation of moderate or greater severity (2/4 or more) or aortic regurgitation of mild or greater severity (1/4 or more); Fisher's exact test was used for the FDA score. Results: 33 people who took MDMA and 29 controls were selected, none with a history of cardiac disease; 4 people in the MDMA group were excluded after scanning (3 for inadequate image quality, 1 for mitral and tricuspid prolapse), leaving 29; all had used MDMA for at least 6 months. 8 people (28%) who took MDMA met the FDA criteria and none of the controls (p = 0.0045); mitral, aortic and tricuspid regurgitation and shape abnormalities were more often seen in the MDMA group (Table 1).

Controls against subjects taking MDMA (n = 29 against 33 for demographics, 29 against 29 for echocardiography). Demographics: women 13 (45%) against 15 (45%); mean age 25.6 (SD 2.6) against 24.3 (SD 3.1) years, p = 0.10; MDMA use in the MDMA group 3.6 (SD 6.7) tablets a week for 6.1 (SD 3.4) years. Echocardiography: mitral insufficiency 2/4 or more 0 against 4 (14%), p = 0.11; mitral regurgitant area ratio 5% (SD 1.3) against 12% (SD 9.8), p < 0.007; mitral restrictive motion 0 against 7 (24%), p = 0.01; mitral strand 0 against 1 (3%); aortic insufficiency 1/4 or more 0 against 4 (14%), p = 0.11; aortic strand 0 against 5 (17%), p = 0.05; tricuspid regurgitation 2/4 or more 0 against 13 (45%), p < 0.001; tricuspid regurgitant area ratio 9% (SD 4.5) against 19% (SD 9.5), p < 0.001; tricuspid restrictive motion 1 (3%) against 5 (17%), p = 0.19; pulmonary regurgitation 1/4 or more 10 (34%) against 14 (48%), p = 0.42. The table also prints relative risks with intervals whose basis is not explained; they are not used here.

evidence.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph (the paragraph beginning 'In the MDMA group, subjects with valvular regurgitation')
evidence.extracted: In the MDMA group, people with mitral or tricuspid regurgitation of 2/4 or more, or any aortic regurgitation, had on average taken more tablets in total (943, SD 1,162) than those with lower grades (242, SD 212), p = 0.03; the group sizes and the way the cumulative number was calculated are not given.

The authors state that this is the first report of valve disease in young adults using or having used MDMA, that valve disease in young adults is very unusual and was not found in their controls, and that strands were seen in the MDMA group and not in the controls. They describe a cell-culture study (Setola et al.) in which MDMA bound to and activated human 5-HT2B receptors and caused prolonged growth responses in human valve cells, and suggest that this may explain valve disease with intermittent use; the present study did not test the mechanism.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 6th paragraph (the paragraph beginning 'Although in our study, regurgitations were hemodynamically most often mild to moderate') and 7th paragraph (the paragraph beginning 'This study has some limitations')
evidence.extracted: The authors write that the regurgitations were most often mild to moderate in their effect on blood flow. Limitations they state: MDMA is illegal and people were difficult to recruit, so the study is relatively small; information about the amount of use came from interrogating the people; there were no echocardiographic data from before MDMA use because a prospective evaluation was not possible for ethical reasons; and there is no pathologic evidence of the valve abnormalities because no valve surgery was needed. They say that further studies should help define the clinical significance and extent of the findings. (The paper also calls its findings of great clinical importance and suggests endocarditis prophylaxis; no data in the paper test those statements.)
evidence.quote: There were no echocardiographic data available before MDMA use

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E overall high on the study card: confounding, exposure measurement and selection each rated high (people recruited from psychiatry departments and drug-help centres against student controls; use reported by interview; other drug use not reported).

indirectness.note: The claim names the people studied and the outcome measured, and states the limits.

imprecision.note: 8 events in 29 people with a wide interval (15% to 46%); several differences rest on 4 or 5 people and are not clear on their own.

grade.reasoning: A cross-sectional comparison starts low (METHODS 6.3); risk of bias and imprecision each take a level, so the result is very low. No upgrade for a large effect (0 of 29 against 8 of 29) or for dose response (943 against 242 tablets) is applied, because confounding and selection are rated high and the dose figures cannot be checked. Status single-study: the paper presents itself as the first report, and this claim does not review later echocardiography studies. The claim is worded as an association in these 58 people, says that cause and any symptoms are untested, and gives no advice.

verification.flag_note: One small study (58 people), cross-sectional although the paper calls it case-control (see the study card). The paper's relative risks and some abstract p values (mitral strand and 1/4 mitral regurgitation) cannot be traced to Table 1; the claim uses counts and Fisher p values only. Later echocardiography studies of people who have taken MDMA were not read for this claim and should be checked before it is published; the cell-culture study (Setola et al., 2003, Mol Pharmacol) has no reference record here.
